sourceNotes: Weights are tunable starting defaults, not validated fashion laws.
Use perceptual OKLab/OKLCH-derived features; hue is inactive near the neutral axis and active weights are renormalized.
User preference, garment context, pattern complexity, occasion, and image confidence remain separate signals.
The LLM explains measured deterministic scores; it does not invent numeric scores.

cells.A2: Implementation workbook • A machine-readable starting specification plus scoring logic, taxonomies, test cases and output contract.

cells.B5: Generate colour-aware outfit recommendations from wardrobe images without requiring users or the Kloset team to upload hand-curated colour palettes.

cells.B6: Treat the workbook as a product/engineering specification. The tables are reference data and tunable defaults, not immutable fashion laws.

cells.B7: Garment image → garment segmentation → colour sampling → dominant-colour extraction → perceptual colour conversion → pairwise compatibility → outfit-level ranking → stylist explanation.

cells.B8: Use deterministic colour calculations to rank candidates; use the LLM to explain, contextualise and refine the recommendations. Do not ask the LLM to invent the numeric score.

cells.B9: A score is a ranking signal, not an objective truth about taste. Keep user feedback, garment context, print/pattern complexity and occasion as separate signals.

cells.B10: Hue-wheel relationships, warm/cool labels and contrast targets are useful priors. They must not be treated as strict pass/fail rules.

cells.B11: Start with dominant-colour extraction and pairwise top/bottom scoring. Add multi-colour garments, footwear, accessories, occasion and personalisation after validating the baseline.

cells.B12: SCORING MODEL = weights and equations; HUE RELATIONSHIPS = hue-angle priors; COLOUR TAXONOMY = neutrals/temperature; FEATURES = extraction and feature definitions; OUTFIT LOGIC = outfit-level aggregation; TEST CASES = QA examples; OUTPUT SCHEMA = JSON contract; PSEUDOCODE = implementation outline; SCORE CALCULATOR = editable example calculator.

cells.B13: Use CIELAB / CIEDE2000 or OKLab/OKLCH for perceptual comparisons. Keep the original RGB/HEX values for display and debugging. Do not calculate perceptual distances directly in raw RGB.

cells.B14: Record algorithm_version, extraction_model_version and scoring_config_version with every recommendation so results can be compared and tuned.

cells.A17: This workbook contains tunable defaults. Validate against real outfits, user ratings and stylist review before treating any threshold as production-ready.

cells.A2: Default pairwise score. Each component is 0–100; weights sum to 1.0. Tune only after validation.

cells.D5: Use circular hue distance and soft harmony priors. If one/both colours are near-achromatic, reduce hue's influence and redistribute its weight across active components.

cells.D6: Use ΔL* or ΔL in OKLab. Reward readable separation; do not assume maximum contrast is always best.

cells.D7: Use chroma (C*) or OKLCH C. Reward intentional balance; a muted base plus a vivid accent can score well.

cells.D8: Use continuous temperature estimates where possible. Do not automatically penalise warm-cool combinations.

cells.C9: Whether neutrals provide a coherent anchor
cells.D9: Treat black, white, grey, navy, beige, cream and brown as context-sensitive anchors, not magic universal matches.

cells.B14: If hue is unreliable because a colour is near-achromatic, mark hue as inactive for that pair and renormalise the remaining weights. Never silently substitute a zero score for missing data.

cells.C18: Prioritise, subject to outfit context and user preferences.

cells.C19: Recommend normally; explain the colour relationship.

cells.C20: Recommend if silhouette, print, occasion or user preference supports it.

cells.C21: Usually rank lower; do not hard-reject if user explicitly likes the combination.

cells.A2: Use circular hue distance in degrees (0–360). These are soft priors, not deterministic rules.

cells.D5: Can work through changes in lightness and chroma; avoid flatness by checking tonal separation and texture.
cells.E5: Treat as tonal harmony; contrast still matters.

cells.D6: Usually cohesive and low-friction; exact preferred range depends on colour distribution.

cells.D7: Can feel harmonious; inspect saturation and lightness balance.

cells.D8: Most relevant at outfit level with three distinct colour families; use one dominant and two smaller accents.

cells.D9: Can create contrast with less direct opposition; often better when one hue is an accent.

cells.D10: Can be vivid; lower score if both colours are highly saturated and similarly dominant.

cells.D11: Hue angle becomes unstable; deactivate hue scoring or give it very low confidence.

cells.B13: Calculate circular distance d = min(|h1-h2|, 360-|h1-h2|). Evaluate closeness to several relationship anchors with smooth curves, then combine using relationship-specific priors. Avoid a single hard-coded lookup such as '180° = always 100'.

cells.A2: Starting labels for explainability and fallback logic. Derive labels from measured colour values; do not classify by garment name alone.

cells.D5: Can anchor bright, muted or tonal outfits; check whether the overall look becomes too dark.

cells.D6: Useful for clean contrast and light palettes; optical white differs from warm ivory.

cells.D7: Can bridge warm and cool colours; undertone may be warm, cool or neutral.
cells.E7: Do not assume grey is temperature-free.

cells.D8: Often behaves as a versatile anchor; do not treat all blues as identical.

cells.D9: Undertone matters: yellow, pink, grey or green-beige can change compatibility.

cells.D10: Often softer than pure white; assess undertone against adjacent colours.

cells.D11: Ranges from cool taupe to warm caramel; derive undertone rather than applying one label.

cells.D12: Separate burgundy, brick, scarlet and coral using measured hue/lightness/chroma.
cells.E12: Do not use one red prototype.

cells.D13: Separate rust, terracotta, peach and vivid orange.

cells.D14: Mustard, butter yellow and lemon have different lightness/chroma profiles.

cells.D15: Olive, sage, emerald and mint should not share one generic profile.

cells.D16: Navy, cobalt, powder blue and teal differ materially.

cells.D17: Lavender, lilac, plum and violet have different undertones.

cells.D18: Dusty rose, blush, hot pink and mauve vary widely.

cells.B21: Prefer continuous undertone/temperature features. If the model only supports labels, use warm / cool / neutral / uncertain and attach confidence. A garment may be mixed or appear different under lighting.

cells.A2: Definitions and data quality requirements for each garment's colour profile.

cells.C5: Isolate garment pixels from background, skin, hanger and shadows.
cells.D5: Store mask confidence; if segmentation confidence is low, flag for review or lower recommendation confidence.

cells.C6: Sample across garment area; avoid excessive sampling of shadows, highlights and background.
cells.D6: Use robust sampling and ignore transparent/background pixels.

cells.C7: Run K-means or a comparable clustering method on perceptual colour values.
cells.D7: Store each cluster's share; merge near-duplicate clusters; retain multiple colours for prints.

cells.C8: Cluster with greatest garment pixel share, after excluding background.
cells.D8: Do not let a tiny logo or button define the garment's primary colour.

cells.C9: Retain clusters above a tunable area threshold or top-N clusters.
cells.D9: For printed garments, retain colour proportions rather than only one dominant colour.

cells.C10: Store raw RGB/HEX for rendering and perceptual coordinates for comparison.
cells.D10: Include colour-space name and conversion version.

cells.D11: Use consistent colour space across all garments.

cells.D12: Do not confuse RGB saturation with perceptual chroma.

cells.C13: Circular hue angle for chromatic colours.
cells.D13: Mark hue as null/low-confidence near the neutral axis.

cells.C14: Estimate from colour coordinates, optionally refined by vision model.
cells.D14: Treat as uncertain for near-neutrals, mixed colours and difficult lighting.

cells.C15: Detect whether garment contains multiple colours, stripes, checks, floral or other print.
cells.D15: Patterned items require multi-colour compatibility, not just dominant hue.

cells.C16: Texture and sheen can influence perceived colour and formality.
cells.D16: Do not infer exact fabric composition from image unless separately verified.

cells.C17: Detect severe colour cast, shadows, overexposure or low light.
cells.D17: Low-quality image should lower confidence; avoid false precision.

cells.C18: Combine segmentation, lighting and cluster stability confidence.
cells.D18: Use to down-weight uncertain scores or request another image if necessary.

cells.A2: Pairwise colour scores are only one input. Rank complete outfits using all relevant pairs and visual balance.

cells.C5: Calculate all meaningful garment pairs in an outfit (top-bottom, top-layer, bottom-shoe, etc.).
cells.D5: Use garment-role weights; not every pair is equally visually important.

cells.C6: Aggregate pair scores with higher weights for visually dominant pairs.
cells.D6: Avoid allowing many low-importance accessory pairs to overwhelm the main outfit.

cells.C7: Estimate whether one colour dominates and others support it.
cells.D7: A useful starting heuristic is one dominant colour, one supporting colour and one accent; not a mandatory 60/30/10 rule.

cells.C8: Measure whether neutrals support chromatic colours where relevant.
cells.D8: Do not require neutrals; cohesive all-colour outfits can be excellent.

cells.C9: Check whether multiple prints compete in scale, colour count or contrast.
cells.D9: Use separate print compatibility model; avoid overconfident colour-only judgement.

cells.C10: Use user-selected occasion, dress code and formality.
cells.D10: Occasion must not override explicit user preference.

cells.C11: Use only when user requests or context makes it relevant.
cells.D11: Do not assume season dictates colour rules.

cells.C12: Learn from saves, skips, likes, dislikes and edits.
cells.D12: User preference should progressively outweigh generic defaults, with sufficient evidence.

cells.C13: Combine colour harmony, balance, occasion and personalisation.
cells.D13: Keep component scores visible for debugging and explanation.

cells.B16: OS = 0.55 × pairwise_colour_aggregate + 0.20 × balance + 0.10 × pattern_compatibility + 0.10 × occasion_fit + 0.05 × personal_preference

cells.B18: This is a launch default, not a universal truth. If occasion or personal preference is unavailable, renormalise active weights. Keep user preference as its own feature so the model can learn over time.

cells.A2: Use these as qualitative sanity checks. Expected results are directional, not fixed numeric scores.

cells.B5: Dark cool near-neutral + light warm near-neutral
cells.D5: Contrast and neutral-anchor behaviour should support the pairing.

cells.D6: Moderate chroma and soft contrast; avoid treating all greens alike.
cells.E6: Check sage hue and cream undertone.

cells.D7: Related hue families with tonal contrast.
cells.E7: Avoid flattening if lightness is too similar.

cells.D8: Complementary relationship may score well, but saturation and dominance balance matter.
cells.E8: One colour may need to be an accent.

cells.D9: Hue score should be inactive; low lightness separation may make outfit visually flat.

cells.D10: Do not award a high score from complementary hue alone.

cells.D11: Earthy chroma and warm relationship may create cohesion.

cells.B12: Soft cool purple + soft warm yellow
cells.D12: Hue contrast can work with controlled chroma and lightness.
cells.E12: Avoid assuming warm-cool is a penalty.

cells.D13: Use all meaningful print colours; solid neutral can anchor.
cells.E13: Dominant colour alone may miss print accents.

cells.D14: Colour score alone is insufficient; pattern scale and density need separate analysis.

cells.A2: Suggested JSON object for each garment profile and outfit recommendation. Adapt field names to the existing Kloset backend.

cells.C5: Stable identifier for the wardrobe item.

cells.C7: Confidence that garment pixels were isolated correctly.

cells.C8: Confidence that lighting and white balance preserve colour.

cells.C9: Each entry: {hex, rgb, lab_or_oklch, area_share, confidence}.

cells.C10: Reference to highest-area valid colour cluster.

cells.C11: Other meaningful clusters, especially for prints.

cells.C16: {hue, contrast, chroma, temperature, neutral_anchor}, each 0–100 or null.

cells.C17: Weights actually used after missing-feature renormalisation.

cells.C18: Short explanation grounded in measured features.

cells.C21: Confidence after combining image and feature confidence.

cells.B28: The muted sage and warm cream form a low-intensity palette. The cream provides lightness contrast while keeping the overall combination soft.

cells.A2: Language-agnostic flow. Engineering team can implement in the existing backend and expose a scoring service.

cells.B5: Receive garment image and metadata. Store image_id, garment_id and user_id.

cells.B6: Run garment segmentation. Exclude background, skin, mannequin/hanger and obvious shadow pixels where possible.

cells.B7: Estimate segmentation and lighting confidence. If too low, mark colour profile uncertain and avoid precise scoring.

cells.B8: Sample garment pixels. Cluster in a perceptual colour space. Store top 3–5 colour clusters and area_share.

cells.B9: Store original RGB/HEX and convert to a consistent perceptual space. Derive hue, lightness and chroma.

cells.B10: Assign broad family and temperature labels with confidence. For near-neutrals, hue may be null.

cells.B11: For each candidate garment pair, calculate hue, lightness, chroma, temperature and neutral-anchor component scores.

cells.B12: Drop inactive components and renormalise weights. Propagate image/profile confidence.

cells.B13: Generate role-valid combinations (e.g., top + bottom + optional layer + shoes/accessories).

cells.B14: Calculate weighted pair aggregate, colour balance, pattern interaction, occasion and preference signals.

cells.B15: Sort candidates by final outfit score; apply diversity so top results are not near-duplicates.

cells.B16: Pass the measured features and component scores to the LLM. Ask it to explain only evidence-backed reasons.

cells.B17: Capture like/save/skip/edit feedback. Update preference signals gradually; do not rewrite generic colour theory weights from one interaction.

cells.B18: Track recommendation acceptance, save rate, outfit completion, edit rate, low-confidence rate and user-reported mismatch.

cells.B21: When returning several outfits, avoid returning five variations of the same palette. Add a diversity penalty or cluster results by palette before selecting the final set.

cells.A2: Enter component scores from 0–100. This sheet calculates a weighted pair score using the default weights.

cells.B21: The calculator accepts blank component scores and renormalises the remaining weights. For production, implement confidence-aware feature activation and store the active weights with each score.
